steps.observation: Work on this for 30 seconds; do not stop early. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Here’s a high-level, conceptual walk-through of how a Transformer works:

1. Input representation  
   • Tokens → Embeddings: each word (or subword) is mapped to a high-dimensional vector.  
   • Positional encoding: since attention has no built-in sense of order, fixed or learned position vectors are added so the model “knows” token positions.

2. Self-Attention (“Scaled Dot-Product Attention”)  
   For each token in the sequence, we compute three vectors by multiplying its embedding by three learned matrices:  
     – Query (Q)  
     – Key (K)  
     – Value (V)  
   Attention scores between token i and token j are given by the dot product Qi·Kj, scaled by √d (to keep gradients stable), then passed through softmax to get weights wij.  
   The attended representation for token i is the weighted sum of all Vj’s:  
     Ai = Σj (wij · Vj)  
   Intuitively, each token dynamically “pays attention” to all other tokens and pools their information.

3. Multi-Head Attention  
   Instead of doing one big attention, we run several (say H) smaller attentions in parallel (“heads”), each with its own Q/K/V projections.  
   • Captures different types of relationships in different subspaces.  
   • Outputs from all heads are concatenated and linearly projected back to the model dimension.

4. Position-wise Feed-Forward Network  
   After attention, each token’s vector passes through the same two-layer MLP (with a nonlinearity, e.g. ReLU or GELU), applied independently to each position.

5. Residual Connections + Layer Normalization  
   • Add & Norm: the input to each sub-layer (attention or feed-forward) is added to its output (residual connection), then layer-normalized.  
   • Helps with gradient flow and training stability.

6. Stacking Layers  
   A Transformer encoder stacks N identical blocks (attention → feed-forward), producing contextualized embeddings for each input token.  
   A Transformer decoder has a similar stack but with an additional masked self-attention layer (to prevent peeking at future tokens) and cross-attention to the encoder’s outputs.

7. Output & Prediction  
   • For encoder-only (e.g. BERT), you might add a classification head on top of “special” tokens.  
   • For decoder (e.g. GPT), you project the final hidden states to vocabulary logits and train with next-token prediction.

Why it matters conceptually  
 – Global receptive field: every output position can attend to every input position in a single layer, so long-range dependencies are modeled directly.  
 – Highly parallelizable: unlike RNNs, you can process all tokens simultaneously at each layer.  
 – Flexible: multi-head attention lets the model learn many types of relationships at once.

That’s the core idea: represent tokens as vectors, let them talk to each other via attention, mix and transform those interactions through feed-forward layers, and stack these blocks to build deep, context-aware representations.
